common_name: Apricot Gold Osmanthus (Apricot-Flowered Sweet Tea Olive)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; Apricot Gold is grown for its warm apricot-orange flower clusters, a shade deeper than the pale yellow of 'Butter Yellow'.

directions: Apricot Gold tea olive is a selection prized for clusters of small, warm apricot-orange flowers that perfume the garden on mild days from fall into winter, a deeper, more peach-toned bloom than the paler 'Butter Yellow' and 'Conger Yellow' selections. It forms a dense, upright evergreen screen or large background shrub with glossy dark green leaves, tolerating part shade well but flowering most heavily with several hours of direct sun. Established plants shrug off summer heat and brief dips into the low 20s F, though flower buds can be lost in harder freezes. Prune lightly after the main flowering flush if a tighter form is wanted; otherwise this cultivar is happiest left to its naturally rounded, slow-to-moderate growth habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center

common_name: French White Laurustinus Viburnum (Heavy-Blooming White Viburnum Tinus)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; French White is an RHS Award of Garden Merit selection grown for unusually heavy clusters of pure white winter-into-spring flowers.

directions: French White laurustinus produces broad, flattened clusters of pure white flowers opening from late winter into spring, held above dense, dark evergreen foliage, and the display is notably fuller than many other Viburnum tinus selections. The shrub builds into a substantial, rounded hedge or screen over a few seasons, taking well to light shearing right after bloom or left loosely informal for a more natural look. It handles heat, humidity, and brief hard freezes once established, though young plants benefit from winter protection in the colder end of its range. Site it where winter fragrance and the occasional small blue-black fruit that follows flowering can be appreciated up close, such as along a path or near a window.

common_name: Bewley's Variegated Laurustinus Viburnum (Cream-Edged Viburnum Tinus)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade; Bewley's Variegated carries a thin, consistent white-to-cream edge on each leaf and is slightly less vigorous than plain-leaved laurustinus.

directions: Bewley's Variegated laurustinus brightens shady corners with its narrow, consistent cream-to-white leaf margin on otherwise typical dark green, leathery foliage, giving year-round interest even between its late-winter flushes of small white-tinged-pink flower clusters. It grows more slowly and stays noticeably smaller and more compact than green-leaved Viburnum tinus selections, making it useful where a full-size laurustinus would outgrow its space. Light shade helps keep the variegation from scorching in peak summer sun, though some direct morning light improves flowering. Trim out any shoots that revert to solid green promptly to keep the variegated pattern strong over time.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

common_name: Glen St. Mary Pittosporum (Upright Green-Leaved Mock Orange)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Glen St. Mary is a solid dark-green, moderately vigorous selection reaching 6-8 feet, taking a more upright habit than the dwarf variegated pittosporum cultivars.

directions: Glen St. Mary pittosporum is an old, solid-green selection named for the Florida nursery town where it was developed, grown for a tidy upright habit and glossy dark leaves rather than variegation or dwarf stature. Its clusters of small, creamy flowers carry the typical orange-blossom fragrance of the species each spring, drawing attention even though the blooms themselves are inconspicuous against the dense foliage. It takes well to shaping as a clipped hedge or screen and tolerates salt spray, wind, and poor coastal soils about as well as any pittosporum cultivar, needing only a light trim after flowering to stay dense from top to bottom. Established plants are drought-tolerant and largely untroubled by pests, though scale can appear on stressed shrubs in deep shade.
sources: Clemson Cooperative Extension Home & Garden Information Center
